title: Hezekiah's Prayer and Sennacherib's Fall
summary: Hezekiah answers the Assyrian threats by going into the temple in sackcloth and sending to Isaiah, who promises that the king of Assyria will hear a rumor and go home. A second, written threat arrives, and Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD and prays that all kingdoms may know that the LORD alone is God. Isaiah sends back a long oracle against Sennacherib's pride, a sign of harvests restored, and a promise that the city will not be touched; that night the angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp, and Sennacherib withdraws to Nineveh, where his own sons later kill him.
story: Chapter 36 ended with Assyria's spokesman, the Rabshakeh, standing outside Jerusalem's walls mocking Judah's trust in its God. Chapter 37 is the answer, and it comes in two rounds of threat and response. The whole first half of Isaiah has asked one question over and over: whom will Judah trust when the great powers close in? Hezekiah's father Ahaz, faced with a smaller crisis in chapter 7, refused the sign Isaiah offered and leaned on Assyria. Hezekiah, facing Assyria itself, goes to the temple, asks for the prophet's prayer, and prays himself. The deliverance of Jerusalem is the high point of the Assyrian story in the book, and it sets up the sobering turn of chapters 38 and 39, where the same king's weakness points ahead to Babylon.
historical:
The setting is Sennacherib's campaign against Judah in 701 BC. Hezekiah had joined a revolt against Assyria after the death of Sargon II in 705 BC, and Sennacherib marched west to crush it. His own royal annals, preserved on clay prisms, list forty-six fortified cities of Judah taken and claim that Hezekiah was shut up in Jerusalem like a caged bird. Tellingly, the annals do not claim that Jerusalem fell. The siege of Lachish, the major fortress southwest of Jerusalem mentioned in verse 8, was carved in detail on the walls of Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh, and those reliefs are now in the British Museum. Excavations at Lachish have also uncovered the Assyrian siege ramp.

Tirhakah (Taharqa) in verse 9 was a ruler of Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty, whose kings came from Cush, the land south of Egypt along the Nile. Egyptian records suggest he did not become king until about 690 BC, so in 701 he was probably a young prince leading the army; most interpreters think the text calls him king by the title he later held, though some propose other solutions. Sennacherib's assassination in verse 38 took place in 681 BC, twenty years after the campaign; a Babylonian chronicle records that he was killed by his son in a rebellion, and Esarhaddon did succeed him. The god Nisroch has not been securely identified.
cultural:
Tearing clothes and wearing sackcloth, a rough goat-hair cloth, were the ordinary signs of mourning and repentance in Israel. When Hezekiah's officials come to Isaiah dressed that way, the court is behaving like a house in mourning. The proverb in verse 3, children at the point of birth with no strength to deliver them, describes a labor that kills both mother and child, and it was as grim to its first hearers as it sounds.

Hezekiah's gesture of spreading the letter before the LORD made sense in a world where the temple was the throne room of the divine King. He addresses God as "enthroned above the cherubim," the winged figures over the ark of the covenant in the inner sanctuary. The Assyrian boast in verses 11 to 13 rests on the common ancient assumption that every city had its gods and that conquering a city proved your gods stronger. Hezekiah's prayer rejects the premise: those gods were destroyed because they were never gods at all. The threat of a hook in the nose borrows from the way conquerors treated captives; Assyrian royal monuments show defeated kings led on cords. Here the image is turned back on Assyria.
literary: Isaiah 36 to 39 runs closely parallel to 2 Kings 18:13 to 20:19, with small differences (Isaiah omits Hezekiah's payment of tribute and adds Hezekiah's psalm in chapter 38). Chapter 37 is built as two matching rounds: a threat (verses 1 to 4, then 9 to 13), a turn to God (Isaiah consulted, then Hezekiah praying), and a divine answer (a brief oracle in verses 6 and 7, then the full oracle in verses 21 to 35). The long answer is itself carefully built. A taunt song (verses 22 to 29) quotes the Assyrian king's boasts back at him and then reveals that God planned his conquests long ago, followed by a sign for Hezekiah (verses 30 to 32) and a promise about the city (verses 33 to 35). The narrative fulfillment in verses 36 to 38 is told in few words, and the closing irony is sharp: the king who mocked the gods of other nations dies in the temple of his own.

outline.t: Hezekiah mourns and Isaiah promises a rumor and a retreat
Hezekiah spreads the letter before the LORD and prays
The LORD's taunt against the proud king of Assyria
A sign for Hezekiah and a promise to defend the city
The Assyrian camp struck and Sennacherib's death

doctrines.note: Hezekiah's prayer is a model of biblical petition. It begins with who God is, the one who made the heavens and the earth, states the danger honestly, and asks for rescue for the sake of God's name among the nations. The oracle then links the answer directly to the prayer: “Because you have prayed to Me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria.”

The taunt song's claim is that even Assyria's victories were within God's plan: “Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it.” The empire that thought it was the author of history turns out to be an instrument, and its arrogance brings it under judgment.

Hezekiah concedes the facts in the Assyrian boast and denies its conclusion. The gods of the conquered nations were “the work of human hands,” so their destruction proved nothing about the living God.

words.note: Charaph, to taunt or reproach. The word runs through the chapter (verses 4, 17, 23, 24) to name what Assyria has really done: not merely threatened a city but insulted the living God. Hezekiah's case before God rests on that. The quarrel is no longer Judah's; it is the LORD's honor that has been challenged.

Palal, to pray, used of Hezekiah in verse 15 and in the LORD's answer in verse 21. The chapter draws a clear line between the prayer and the deliverance, which is one reason it became a classic text on intercession in times of national danger.

She'erit, remnant. Hezekiah asks Isaiah to pray for “the remnant that still survives” (verse 4), and the oracle promises that “a remnant will go forth from Jerusalem” (verse 32). With most of Judah's cities taken, the idea that God preserves a surviving core of his people, prominent throughout Isaiah, is suddenly concrete.

Ganan, to defend or shield. “I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.” The reason given is not Jerusalem's merit but God's name and his promise to David's house.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ runs through two threads rather than a direct prediction. The first is the promise to David. God saves the city “for the sake of My servant David,” holding to the covenant that David's line would endure (2 Samuel 7), and the New Testament presents Jesus as the Son of David in whom that covenant finds its lasting king. The second is the remnant: the image of the surviving house of Judah that will “take root below and bear fruit above” echoes Isaiah's earlier picture of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (11:1), which the church has read of the Messiah. More broadly, Hezekiah's prayer that all the kingdoms of the earth may know the LORD anticipates the mission of the gospel to the nations. These are thematic connections, and the chapter should first be read as what it is: a real deliverance in 701 BC.

hard.q: Did an angel really kill 185,000 Assyrian soldiers in one night, and what does history say?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real on two fronts: the scale of death, and the lack of any Assyrian record of disaster. On the second point, Assyrian royal inscriptions did not report defeats, so their silence is expected; what they do show is that Sennacherib took Lachish and many cities, yet never claims to have captured Jerusalem or deposed Hezekiah, which is striking for a king who routinely did both to rebels. The Greek historian Herodotus, writing in the fifth century BC, preserves an Egyptian story that Sennacherib's army withdrew after mice gnawed its equipment in the night, which some connect with a plague. Many interpreters who read the account as history think God used an epidemic in the camp; others simply take the text as describing a direct act of God. Some scholars read the number and the angel as a later heightening of a real, unexpected withdrawal. Readers also debate whether Hebrew 'eleph (thousand) here can mean a military unit, which would lower the figure, though this is uncertain.

The moral question is the one raised by every judgment in Scripture. The text presents the event not as random slaughter but as God's judgment on an empire that had destroyed nation after nation and now openly defied him. It is told soberly, with no celebration: the people rose in the morning and found the dead.

questions: Hezekiah spread the threatening letter before God and read it there. What would it look like to bring a specific fear to God in that concrete way?
The Assyrian king believed his victories were his own achievement. Where are people, or nations, tempted to read their success as proof of their own greatness?
Hezekiah's request was that all the kingdoms of the earth might know the LORD. How does it change a prayer for rescue when its goal is God's name rather than our own safety?
